name: Livagen

lead: Livagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala) is a short peptide from Khavinson's group in Russia, described as a regulator of gene activity in ageing cells. Forum users pitch it as a non-injectable-style anti-aging option meant to keep cells acting younger and, in turn, looking younger.

The chain runs from chromatin and gene-expression effects to cells behaving younger to a younger appearance. Researchers report that it loosens condensed heterochromatin and activates ribosomal genes in lymphocytes from older donors, and stimulates liver tissue growth in culture. Studies are small and mostly in cell cultures and rats; skin, hair and bone have not been tested in people.

paras: It is used in periodic courses as part of broader longevity stacks, often with other bioregulator peptides. Users describe expecting slow, cumulative effects over months.
No human safety data was found. It is sold online as a research peptide rather than an approved medicine, so product purity and legal status vary by country.

angle.text: Livagen is pitched by forum users as a peptide that makes cells act younger, which they hope shows up as younger-looking skin, hair and tissue. Lab work reports chromatin changes in cells from older donors; visible ageing has not been tested in people.

lead: Livagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the sequence Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala (KEDA), developed in Russia as one of the short peptide bioregulators associated with Vladimir Khavinson and the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology.[1][2][3]

People interested in looks encounter it as an anti-ageing peptide. The idea, as presented in forum guides, is that a molecule which switches on 'youthful' gene activity could slow, or even partly reverse, ageing of skin, bone and hair, so that someone keeps a younger appearance for longer.[4] That is a chain of reasoning from laboratory chromatin findings to appearance outcomes; the intermediate steps have not been tested in people.

Its published research is mainly laboratory work on chromatin in lymphocytes from elderly donors, along with rat studies on tissue growth and digestive enzymes. Authors report that it activates ribosomal genes and loosens condensed heterochromatin.[5][6] No controlled human trials of its effects on appearance or ageing were found.
infobox: St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, Russia

paras: Livagen is one of several short peptides, with Epitalon, Vilon, Cortagen and others, that the Khavinson group describes as tissue-specific. In organotypic culture of rat tissue, Livagen was reported to stimulate growth of liver explants, while the others stimulated brain cortex, thymus and other tissue.[2]

Livagen belongs to a family of short peptides promoted by Vladimir Khavinson (1946-2024), a Russian gerontologist who directed the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology.[3] His group's work began in the 1970s with polypeptide complexes extracted from animal organs and, according to Wikipedia's account of his career, produced more than 20 extracted complexes and about 15 synthesised ones by 2013, with several preparations approved for medical use in the USSR, Russia and other CIS countries.[3] The same article lists Livagen and Epitalon among his notable peptides and records counts of 196 patents and 775 publications credited to him, figures that originate with the researcher's own side; Wikipedia tags that section as containing promotional content.[3]

Khavinson's proposed principle is that short peptides of two to four amino acids act as tissue-specific regulators of gene expression, each tuned to an organ: in one 2001 organotypic culture paper, the peptides Cortagen, Epithalon, Livagen and Vilon were reported to stimulate growth of rat brain cortex, subcortical, liver and thymus explants respectively.[2] Livagen is the liver-associated member of the set.[2]

Khavinson was born in 1946 and died in Saint Petersburg on 6 January 2024. Wikipedia lists his roles as director of the Saint Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and head of the gerontology chair at North-Western State Medical University, and records a 2016 Russian Order of Friendship; his books include Peptides and Ageing (2002) and Gerontological Aspects of Genome Peptide Regulation (2005) [3].
Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, lists the molecular formula C18H31N5O9 and a molar mass of about 461.5 g/mol, and notes that it is supplied for research as a lyophilized powder.[1]

The peptide emerged from Russian programs that began in the 1970s with animal-organ polypeptide extracts and moved to defined synthetic peptides in the late 1990s and early 2000s, according to Grokipedia.[1] Early papers on Livagen date to 2001-2002, including studies in tissue culture and in lymphocytes from older people.[5][2]

Reports from the Khavinson group describe Livagen as acting on chromatin, the packaged form of DNA. In lymphocytes cultured from elderly donors, they report that Livagen increased activity of ribosomal genes, lowered measures of heterochromatin condensation and altered the pattern of structural C-heterochromatin, which they interpret as reactivation of genes silenced during ageing.[5][6][7] A 2023 paper from the same research tradition describes epigenetic modification of condensed 'old' chromatin by Livagen, Epitalon and other peptide bioregulators.[8]

Other cell-level findings in the literature include a study of how Livagen affects enkephalin-degrading enzymes in human serum (2003), and papers in lymphocytes from patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and their relatives, and from older people exposed to radiation-induced adaptive-response conditions.[9][10][11] These are in vitro observations on blood cells and do not describe changes in skin, hair or bone.

A 2002 report found that Livagen activated ribosomal genes, decondensed pericentromeric heterochromatin and released genes repressed by age-related condensation in lymphocytes from older individuals.[5] A 2007 paper in cultured lymphocytes from people aged 80 to 91 and young controls looked at Livagen combined with cobalt chloride and at heterochromatin condensation.[12] A 2004 study compared several peptides including Livagen on chromatin in subjects aged 75 to 88.[6] A 2005 rat study examined digestive enzyme activity,[13] and a 2020 paper examined the polypeptide liver complex and KEDA in normal and age-related pathology.[14] These were published mostly in Russian and Georgian journals and are in cell cultures or animals.

Almost all published Livagen work comes from Russian and Georgian research groups, published in a small set of regional journals (Bulletin of Experimental Biology and Medicine, Georgian Medical News, Advances in Gerontology). Wikipedia's article on Khavinson does not describe independent evaluation of the peptide programme, and the PubMed records for Livagen show few citations from outside it.[3][5][8]

Outside Russia, short peptides of this type are sold by online research-peptide vendors as lyophilised powders labelled for laboratory use, and they are not approved as medicines in the US or EU. A looksmax.org reply asks for 'non-injectables' and the guide thread is where Livagen is discussed; in the published studies, exposure was by adding the peptide to cell cultures rather than by dosing people.[4]

No studies found. The human work found uses blood lymphocytes grown in culture rather than treating people.[5][12][6] Reports on lymphocytes from people with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and from old individuals likewise describe cultured cells taken from participants, not an intervention given to them.[10][11]

lore.intro: A looksmax.org mini-guide presents Livagen as a bioregulator that influences DNA activity to make cells act younger.[4]
